687.title: The garden
687.hook: gardens under which rivers flow, and peace as the greeting there (10:10)
687.howItsDone: Muslims greet each other with as-salamu 'alaykum, peace be upon you, the greeting the Qur'an gives to the people of the garden, and end each prayer with it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: raji'un, returning, and your line, a return. Today, where the Qur'an says the return leads, the last of the book's great themes.

Gardens beneath which rivers flow. This path met that phrase on the day about water, and the Qur'an comes back to it again and again when it speaks of what follows death. Shade that doesn't move. Water that doesn't run out. Fruit within reach. A picture anyone can see with their eyes shut. And yet the book says the real thing is hidden. What it does tell, very plainly, is what people there say to each other. One word, and it's an ordinary one.

The word is jannah, a garden. It comes from the root j-n-n, to cover or hide. A garden is a place covered by trees, shaded from view. The same root gives jinn, beings hidden from sight; janin, a child hidden in the womb; and junnah, a shield. So paradise, in Arabic, sounds like a covered, sheltered place. The root fits a promise the book keeps. Surah thirty-two says no soul knows what delight is kept hidden for them. A hadith qudsi in al-Bukhari has Allah say: I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has imagined. The rivers and the shade are pictures; the reality, the hadith says, is beyond them. Then surah Yunus, verse ten, gives the sound of the place. In Pickthall's translation: "and their greeting therein will be: Peace." Salam. In surah fifty-six, the people of the garden hear no idle talk and no sin, only the words peace, peace. In surah thirty-six, peace is a word sent to them from a merciful Lord. Here's the quiet surprise. Muslims say as-salamu 'alaykum, peace be upon you, when they meet, and at the end of every prayer. The greeting the book gives the garden is already in daily use. In this vocabulary, a salam on a street corner is an echo of the garden.

Close your eyes and let a garden come, shade, water moving somewhere close, nothing you have to do; don't build it too carefully, since the hadith says the real one is beyond imagining. Picture someone you love walking toward you there, where the only word either of you needs is salam, peace, and let that word sit in your chest.
Jannah. The garden, from j-n-n, covered and sheltered: rivers beneath, delights still hidden, and peace as the greeting there. Today's word.
Your line: their greeting is peace. Next, eight days of the prophets' own prayers. See you tomorrow.

688.title: Adam's du'a
688.hook: our Lord, we have wronged ourselves (7:23)
688.howItsDone: Muslims learn Adam's du'a (7:23) as one of the Qur'an's prayers for forgiveness; some say it in the prostration or after the prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday: jannah, the garden, and your line, their greeting is peace. The great themes are done. Now, eight days with the prophets' own prayers, starting where the garden story starts.

A plate in pieces on the kitchen floor, and two people standing over it. Before anyone reaches for a broom, somebody speaks. Two sentences are always waiting in that moment. It wasn't my fault. Or: that was me. In the Qur'an's garden story, two creatures get something badly wrong, and each reaches for one of those sentences. One argues his case. The other, Adam, with his wife beside him, turns his sentence into a prayer.
screen: `NOT MY FAULT, OR THAT WAS ME?`

segments.voice: Surah al-A'raf tells it. Iblis is commanded to bow to Adam and refuses. His reason: I am better than him; You made me from fire and him from clay. Later, sent out, he says: because You have led me astray. Blame upward, blame outward. Then Adam and his wife eat from the tree they'd been told to leave alone. And in verse twenty-three, in Pickthall's translation: "They said: Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If Thou forgive us not and have not mercy on us, surely we are of the lost!" Three things. First, they. Both pray it together; the Qur'an doesn't put the blame on her. Second, ourselves. Not Satan, who whispered to them, not the tree, not each other. The wrong is named as damage done to their own souls. Third, the request is only forgiveness and mercy, with nothing bargained. Al-Baqarah says Adam received words from his Lord, and Allah turned to him in forgiveness. Some commentators say those words were this very prayer: Allah taught Adam how to come back, and then accepted it. In Islamic teaching, that forgiveness closed the matter. The Qur'an says no soul carries another's burden, so Adam's children are each born free of his slip. The garden story ends, in the Qur'an, not with a curse but with a returned prayer. Du'a, the word for this kind of personal prayer, means a call. Adam's call is three words long at its heart: rabbana zalamna anfusana.

Let one recent wrong of yours come to mind, small is fine, and notice the excuse that usually comes with it; set the excuse down beside you. If you pray, say Adam's words once, slowly: rabbana zalamna anfusana, our Lord, we have wronged ourselves. If not, say the plain version to yourself: that was mine.
Adam's du'a. Rabbana zalamna anfusana: our Lord, we have wronged ourselves. A prayer that owns the wrong, answered with forgiveness. Today's word.
Your line: we wronged ourselves. The garden story ends with a prayer returned. Day six hundred eighty-eight, done.

689.title: Ibrahim's du'a
689.hook: make me and my children keep the prayer, and accept my prayer (14:40)
689.howItsDone: Some Muslims recite Ibrahim's du'a (14:40–41) in the final sitting of the prayer, before the closing salam, asking for themselves, their children and their parents.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Adam's du'a, rabbana zalamna anfusana, and your line, we wronged ourselves. Today, a prayer from a man at the other end of a long life.

Ibrahim has done almost everything a person of faith could do. He broke the idols. He walked out of the fire. He left his wife and baby in an empty valley on Allah's word. With his son Isma'il, he raised the walls of the Ka'bah, stone by stone. If anyone had earned the right to feel sure of himself, it's him. And at the end of his prayer in surah fourteen, he still asks to be kept, and to be accepted.

Surah Ibrahim, verse forty, in Pickthall's translation: "My Lord! Make me to establish proper worship, and some of my posterity (also); our Lord! and accept the prayer." Two requests. The first: make me keep up the prayer, me and my children after me. Not make me rich, not make me remembered. Keep me praying, and keep them praying. He asks for himself first. Even Ibrahim doesn't assume he'll stay steady on his own. The second is today's line: wa taqabbal du'a', and accept my prayer. Asking isn't the end of it. He asks for the asking to be received. In the next verse he widens the circle: our Lord, forgive me, and my parents, and the believers, on the day the reckoning is set up. Here's the scholar's thread. He says the same kind of thing in al-Baqarah, verse one twenty-seven, while the walls of the Ka'bah are going up: our Lord, accept from us. Commentators record that an early pious man, Wuhayb ibn al-Ward, wept when he recited it: the Friend of the Merciful is building Allah's own House, and he's afraid it won't be accepted. In both places, Ibrahim doesn't treat a good deed as finished just because it's done. Some Muslims recite these verses, fourteen forty and forty-one, in the last sitting of their prayer, so the prayer ends asking for itself to be accepted.

Bring your family to mind one by one, parents, children, siblings, a partner, and picture each in a quiet moment of their own, praying, pausing, or looking for meaning in their way. If you pray, ask for each by name, as Ibrahim did, that they keep their prayer, then add his last words: and accept my prayer. If you don't, simply wish each of them steadiness.
Ibrahim's du'a. Make me and my children keep the prayer, and accept my prayer: the builder of the Ka'bah, still asking to be accepted. Today's word.
Your line: accept my prayer. A good deed still asks to be received. Until tomorrow.

690.title: Musa's du'a at the well
690.hook: my Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send me (28:24)
690.howItsDone: Some Muslims say Musa's du'a (28:24) in times of need, job searches, or uncertainty, leaving the shape of the answer to Allah.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ibrahim's du'a, and your line, accept my prayer. Today, a prayer from a man with nothing left in his hands.

Musa is running. In Egypt, he stepped into a fight to defend a man of his people, struck the other man once, and the man died. Now Pharaoh's people are looking for him. He leaves alone, heading toward Madyan, with only a hope: maybe my Lord will guide me on the right road, he says. He arrives at a well, exhausted. And before he does anything for himself, he notices two young women standing back from the crowd.

Surah al-Qasas, verses twenty-three and twenty-four. A crowd of shepherds is watering their flocks. Two women hold their animals back. Musa asks what's wrong. They say: we can't water until the shepherds have gone, and our father is a very old man. So he waters their flock for them. Then he turns aside into the shade, and there, in Pickthall's translation, he prays: "My Lord! I am needy of whatever good Thou sendest down for me." Look how little he specifies. Not food, though he's hungry. Not safety, though he's hunted. Not a home or a wife. Just: whatever good You send, I need it. The Arabic word is faqir, poor, in need. And khayr, good, is left wide open. He doesn't tell Allah what the answer should look like. And the order: first he helps, then he sits in the shade and asks. The answer comes in the very next verse. One of the two women comes back, walking shyly, and says: my father invites you, to reward you for watering for us. Food, shelter, work, and later a marriage. The Qur'an doesn't name the old father; some commentators said he was the prophet Shu'ayb, and others disagreed. What the verses do show is how much good can arrive through one open request, prayed in the shade, by a tired man who had just helped two strangers.
screen: `HE WATERS, THEN SITS IN THE SHADE.`

Loosen it, and hold the need open. If you pray, say Musa's words, rabbi inni lima anzalta ilayya min khayrin faqir, my Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send me; if not, just sit with open hands.

691.title: Ayyub's du'a
691.hook: harm has touched me, and You are the most merciful (21:83)
691.howItsDone: Muslims who are ill, or praying for someone who is, often recite Ayyub's du'a (21:83); visiting the sick is a strongly encouraged practice in Islam.

segments.voice: Yesterday: faqir, in need, and Musa's open prayer in the shade. Your line was in need of any good. Today, a prayer from someone who'd lost far more.

Hospital waiting rooms have their own language. Some people go silent. Some rage. Some bargain: if you fix this, I'll do anything. Ayyub, Job, was struck by illness, and commentators say he lost his wealth and his family too. Stories people tell describe years of it, in vivid detail; the Qur'an gives no number and no gore. What it does give is the prayer he finally prays. A single verse, and it doesn't ask for anything.

Surah al-Anbiya, verse eighty-three, in Pickthall's translation: Ayyub cries to his Lord, "Lo! adversity afflicteth me, and Thou art Most Merciful of all who show mercy." In Arabic: anni massaniya d-durr, wa anta arhamu r-rahimin. Two statements, side by side. Harm has touched me. And You are the most merciful of the merciful. That's all. He doesn't say heal me, or why me. He doesn't list what he's lost. He tells the truth about his pain and the truth about Allah, and leaves the two next to each other. Scholars have long pointed to this as a model of courtesy in asking, adab: the need laid out, the mercy named, and the One who's merciful trusted to connect them. The verb is massa, to touch: harm has touched me, the Qur'an's ordinary word for affliction reaching someone, used without drama. The next verse gives the answer: We heard him, removed the harm, and restored his family to him, and the like of them with them, a mercy from Us and a reminder for those who worship. Surah Sad adds the scene. He's told: strike the ground with your foot; here is cool water to wash in and to drink. And Allah describes him: We found him patient; how excellent a servant; he was always turning back. Patience, in Ayyub, isn't silence. It's saying the hard thing and the true thing in one breath, and not letting go of either.
screen: `ADAB: SAY THE NEED, NAME THE MERCY.`

segments.voice: Let someone who is ill come to mind, in body, in mind, or in grief, and picture them where they are right now, a bed, a waiting room, a kitchen, without rushing to fix it. If you pray, recite Ayyub's own words from 21:83 while you hold them in mind; if you don't, hold both truths: they're hurting, and they're not alone.
Ayyub's du'a. Harm has touched me, and You are the most merciful of the merciful: a prayer that names the pain and the mercy, and asks nothing more. Today's word.
Your line: you are the most merciful. The pain and the mercy, side by side. Day six hundred ninety-one, done.

692.title: Yunus's du'a
692.hook: there is no god but You, glory to You, I was wrong (21:87)
692.howItsDone: Some Muslims recite the du'a of Yunus, la ilaha illa anta subhanaka inni kuntu min az-zalimin, in times of distress, sometimes many times over, and some gatherings recite it together when someone is in trouble.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ayyub's du'a, harm has touched me, and You are the most merciful. Today, a prophet in the dark, and a way back.

Night. Deep water. And inside a great fish, a man. The Qur'an doesn't give the size of the fish or how long he stayed. It gives the prayer. The man is Yunus, the one the Bible calls Jonah, and surah twenty-one gives him a nickname: Dhu'n-Nun, the one of the fish. He had gone off in anger, the verse says, thinking he would not be hemmed in; commentators read that phrase more than one way. Now there is nowhere left to walk. So he calls out from the darkness, in three short clauses.

Surah twenty-one, verse eighty-seven, in Pickthall's translation: "There is no God save Thee. Be Thou Glorified! Lo! I have been a wrong-doer." Look at the order. First, there is no god but You: before he asks for anything, he says who he is talking to. Second, glory to You, subhanak: You are above any blame. Third, I was wrong. The Arabic is min az-zalimin, one of the wrongdoers. Its root, z-l-m, gives zulm, injustice, which the classical dictionaries explain as putting a thing where it doesn't belong. It's the same root as Adam's zalamna, four days ago. And notice what's missing. He doesn't blame his stubborn people, or the ship's crew who cast lots, or the fish. He doesn't even ask to be let out. The asking is folded inside the admitting. The next verse gives the answer: Allah heard him and saved him from his distress, and this, the verse says, is how He saves the believers. Surah thirty-seven adds that if Yunus had not been one who glorified Allah, he would have stayed inside the fish until the day of rising. A hadith in al-Tirmidhi calls this the du'a of Dhu'n-Nun, and says no Muslim prays with it for anything without being answered. So Muslims who know it turn to it in tight places: a hospital corridor, a debt, a night that won't end.

`THEN: GLORY TO YOU, ABOVE ANY BLAME.`

If you don't, sit with the last three words alone, let one small thing come to mind where they're true, and set it down in the dark without arguing or explaining.
Yunus's du'a. Three clauses from the belly of the fish: there is no god but You, glory to You, I was wrong. The hadith calls it the du'a of Dhu'n-Nun. Today's word.
Your line: I was wrong. Said plainly, with no but after it. See you tomorrow.

693.title: Zakariyya's du'a
693.hook: don't leave me alone, You are the best of inheritors (21:89)
693.howItsDone: Some couples hoping for a child recite Zakariyya's du'a from 21:89 and 3:38, and some Muslims also say its plea not to be left alone in times of loneliness.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Yunus in the dark, and your line, I was wrong. Today, an old man in a quiet room, asking for what looks impossible.

A sanctuary, a prayer chamber the Qur'an calls the mihrab. An old prophet named Zakariyya, the one the Bible calls Zechariah, is the guardian of a girl dedicated to God: Maryam. Surah three says that whenever he went in to her, he found food beside her that he hadn't brought. Where does this come from, he asks. From Allah, she says. And right there, the verse says, Zakariyya prayed. His hair is white. His wife has never had a child. He has no one to carry on after him. Watching that girl, he asks anyway.

The Qur'an tells his prayer more than once. Surah nineteen says he called in secret: my bones have grown weak, my head is shining with gray. Surah twenty-one gives it in one line. In Pickthall's translation: "My Lord! Leave me not childless, though Thou art the best of inheritors." Pickthall writes childless, and that is the sense. But the Arabic word is fardan: alone, single, one by himself. So the plea underneath is today's line: don't leave me alone. Then the second half, easy to hear past. You are the best of inheritors. Everything a person leaves behind, a name, a house, a life's work, ends up with someone. Zakariyya says the One who finally inherits everything is Allah. Commentators have read that half as trust: if a son does not come, what I am is still not lost. So the prayer holds two things at once. He asks plainly for what he wants, and says ahead of time that he won't be abandoned even if the answer is no. The next verse says the answer was yes. Allah heard him, gave him Yahya, John, and made his wife able to bear a child. Then a detail about the whole family: they hurried to do good, and called on Allah in longing and in awe. Lonely people are not rare in this book. Yunus in the fish. Ayyub in his sickness. Zakariyya in an empty house. Each of them speaks, and each is heard.
screen: `MY BONES ARE WEAK, MY HEAD IS GRAY.`
`HEARD: YAHYA, AND A FAMILY THAT HURRIED.`

segments.voice: Bring one person to mind who is more alone than they let on, an older neighbor, a friend far from home, someone newly widowed, and picture where they are right now. If you pray, ask for them in your own words, or borrow Zakariyya's: don't leave them alone. If you don't, keep them company in your mind for the length of the sit.

Zakariyya's du'a. Don't leave me alone; You are the best of inheritors. This week ran from the garden's greeting of peace to Adam, Ibrahim, Musa, Ayyub, Yunus and Zakariyya: prophets, each praying in his own trouble. Today's word.
Your line: don't leave me alone. He asked plainly, and trusted either way. Day six hundred ninety-three, and counting.

chat.says: Zakariyya was old and had no child. What did he ask for?
options: Don't leave me alone, and You are the best of inheritors either way.
To make Maryam his heir, since he had raised her in the sanctuary.
Nothing; he accepted his age and never asked for a child.
chat.meaning: 21:89: Leave me not childless, though Thou art the best of inheritors. Fardan means alone; he asks plainly, and trusts either way.
